 President Donald Trump has questioned why a steep drop in U.S. gas prices came only after Republicans suffered a bruising defeat in the midterm elections. "Biggest drop in gasoline in 18 years. Notice that they waited until after the 'Election?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday. Trump was responding to reports that last Wednesday saw the largest single-day drop in gas prices in 18 years. The national average price of regular gasoline stood at $3.78 a gallon on Tuesday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), marking the first time the price has dropped below $4 since July. Prices vary significantly across the country, ranging from $3.09 per gallon in North Carolina to $5.60 in Hawaii. Bloomberg energy columnist Javier Blas had noted that Wednesday saw the largest single-day drop in gas prices in 18 years and Thursday the second-largest. Blas added: “If (yes, a big if) the wholesale market holds at current levels, American gasoline retail prices would be at a 8-month low by Thanksgiving weekend.” Will Prices Continue Falling? The midterms saw Democrats secure sweeping victories across the country, with voters citing affordability and the cost of living as key issues. Gas prices rose sharply after the war with Iran began in February, as the conflict disrupted oil supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump has acknowledged that the unpopular war had contributed to Republicans’ electoral defeat. The president’s Truth Social post insinuated that gas prices were somehow deliberately kept high in the lead up to the election, though he provided no evidence for his claim. However, gas prices had already begun falling in the weeks before the election, with analysts citing factors including reduced seasonal demand and the completion of refinery maintenance helping boost fuel production. Gas prices have continued to drop further in November, as crude oil ​prices have also fallen amid growing optimism that the U.S. would not resume major military operations against Iran. Trump himself has said that the war was “militarily, effectively over.” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, previously told Newsweek that increased oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks had further helped ease pressure on energy prices. Oil exports from the region have recovered as Gulf producers have adapted shipping practices, despite the continued threat to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. However, De Haan said he believed that gas prices “won’t return to pre-war levels until there’s months and months of de facto oil shipments and no escalations, attacks, and so on—or a deal with Iran.” Despite the recent declines, prices remain unusually high for this time of year. This month is so far the most expensive November on record for gas prices, AAA said, compared with an average price of $3.08 for a gallon of gasoline a year ago.
